beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. This is how Walker is meant to be asked: hand it a game design document, get back a playable Godot project. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction, not a transcript, because this game was rebuilt first, and its document came after.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a vertical shooter — fly a wisp up three ruined city streets, shoot the monster army marching down at you, and defeat the Cerberus at the city gate — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: What happened: a two-stage Unity shooter was rebuilt in Godot first.
GDD.md was written afterwards, from the evidence.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: The Design Document

beats.narration_text: Stage Runner came before its design document. It rebuilds a two-stage Unity shooter where one touch ended the game, and finishes it with lives, drops and a boss. The document was written last, and nothing in it is signed off.

props.text:
Stage Runner
was built from its GDD.
Nothing is signed off.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished six-line text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: The document opens by separating six kinds of claim: recovered from the Unity code, invented for the rebuild, built, observed, proposed, or still waiting on a person. Built: fourteen scripts and a shader. Observed: the game's own playtest passes, and sixty-two assertions pass in this film's three scripted takes. Human playtests: zero.

beats.narration_text: The vision is a proposal: fly a lone wisp up three ruined streets, thin out an army that keeps marching, and win the city back from the Cerberus. Who it's for is left open. The three pillars are read off the code: always firing, the street keeps coming, and one mistake costs while three end it.

beats.narration_text: Here's the core loop on the real build, played by a script, not a person. The countdown. Hold fire and line up under the army; kills become points. At the goal, stage clear, and the card totals the run. Every step is a cut from one take, in order.

beats.narration_text: Four experience goals, all proposed, each with a test a person has to run. The captures can only hint. The script cleared stage one in thirty-one seconds of play and stage two in thirty-eight, without losing a life. But it sees every monster's position, every frame. That's not a first-time player.

beats.narration_text: Movement is a straight port. Unity moved at five units a second, and one unit is seventy-two pixels, so the wisp moves at three hundred and sixty. What changed is the box: Unity clamped to the whole camera, the rebuild to a six hundred and forty pixel street. And holding Shift, new, halves the speed.

beats.narration_text: Unity's enemy script had one set of defaults: three health, a hundred points, one unit a second. Every other value lived in prefabs that never arrived. So the rebuild authored thirteen monsters, from two to six health and sixty-two to a hundred and ninety-five pixels a second, with four ways to move.

beats.narration_text: In Unity, one touch was the whole game: show the game-over screen, and stop time. The rebuild gives three lives a stage. A hit flashes the street red and gives one point six seconds of invulnerability, and a mercy rule clears every fireball, so one hit never chains into the next.

beats.narration_text: The failure path, on purpose: the script flies into monsters without firing. Red flash, a heart goes dark, the wisp blinks. The third touch, and game over, with Unity's crying face. Try Again reloads the stage.

beats.narration_text: The goals are a quiet gap. Unity's game manager checks the score against a goal score, but that number was set in the editor, and the scene files never arrived. So two thousand and four thousand are the rebuild's choices, not recovered values. The document says so.

beats.narration_text: The boss is new. A hundred and ten health, five thousand points. It walks in shielded, then repeats four attacks: an aimed fan, a ring, another fan, and two minions. At half health it's enraged: faster, with wider fans and fuller rings.

beats.narration_text: Menus port Unity's buttons, with one change on purpose. Unity's restart always went back to stage one. The rebuild restarts the stage you're on. It adds keys: Escape or P to pause, M for sound, and R to restart from a menu. That last one has a bug.

show.event: portrait card: Restart Means This Stage

beats.narration_text: Escape, then R. On screen, the stage simply restarts. In the log, Godot reports a script error at line six oh six: the restart call has already removed the scene, so the next line has no viewport.

beats.narration_text: The world is one painted street per stage, scrolling down, with a mirrored copy so the seam always matches. The art is the source folder's: three paintings, a bullet, a crying face, a pack of pixel monsters. The sound isn't. Unity had an audio source and no audio files, so all of it was synthesized.

beats.narration_text: Under the hood, every scene is thin. A stage scene file is seven lines; it sets one number. Eight seconds into stage one, the running stage holds a hundred and thirteen nodes, all built in code. Out of scope, by decision: more stages, difficulty settings, online scores.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: Seven Lines, 113 Nodes

show.event: portrait card: Seven Lines, 113 Nodes

beats.narration_text: The risks section is candid. Nobody has played this by hand, and the Windows build has never run. The capture found the restart error, and one mismatch: the comment says monsters spawn within four and a half units of centre, but the code uses two hundred and eighty-eight pixels, which is four. Five open questions remain for a person.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: What a Person Still Has to Decide

show.event: portrait card: What a Person Still Has to Decide

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This document organizes; it doesn't approve. The loop runs end to end on real input, from the menu to the boss, and to defeat and retry. The rebuild's own additions are labelled. One script error and one wrong comment slipped past the game's own test. What's left is a person's call: the audience, the goals, and whether stage two is fair.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude with your own design document: Here is my game's design document. Pick one proposed experience goal. Rewrite it as a hypothesis with a test I can run with three players, and tell me which result would make me change the design. If no result would change your mind, it isn't a hypothesis yet. Liam, in for Bear.
